```{r setup, include=FALSE}
## ── Reproducibility switch (set in the YAML header) ──────────────────────────
##   params$recompute = FALSE : load the dual-regime rolling calibration from its
##                              cache (default).
##                    = TRUE  : re-run it and refresh the cache. Everything else is
##                              either computed live (the SSE surfaces, the data and
##                              the single-model calibrations) or always loaded from
##                              its pre-computed .rds (the noise tables and the S&P 500
##                              rolling calibration; see "Reproducibility").
RECOMPUTE <- isTRUE(params$recompute)

## Pre-computed .rds live in a subdirectory next to this file. It is located from
## the input file, not the working directory, because some ways of knitting
## (polymode's ESS exporter among them) knit in the R session's working
## directory. Run interactively, chunk by chunk, it falls back to the working
## directory.
input_dir <- if (is.null(knitr::current_input())) "." else
  dirname(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE))
DATA_DIR  <- file.path(input_dir, "lpplsF_guide_data")
dpath     <- function(f) file.path(DATA_DIR, f)
if (RECOMPUTE) dir.create(DATA_DIR, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 110, fig.align = "center")

library(lpplsF)
suppressMessages(library(ggplot2))
```

`lpplsF` fits the **log-periodic power-law singularity (LPPLS)** model of Sornette
and co-authors — a model of the faster-than-exponential, log-periodically
decorated price growth that can precede a financial-bubble crash. This document
is a **guided tour of the package**: every calibration, diagnostic and plot it
offers, worked through on a series of examples that build on one another.

**How to read it.** Each section builds on the previous one, from a single
calibration on simulated data, through the optimizer's behaviour and its
sensitivity to noise, to rolling-window bubble-onset detection and finally a real
market series. You can read it front to back, or jump to the section matching the
function you need.

**Theory, and where to find it.** This guide is about *using* the package; it
assumes the model rather than deriving it. The accompanying master's thesis sets
out the theory behind every method used here: the model's derivation, the
calibration scheme, the modified profile likelihood and the Lagrange
regularization. Each section below names the thesis figure it corresponds to, so
you can read the two side by side.

**Reproducibility.** The single-model calibrations run live every time the
document is knitted. The multi-fit noise and rolling-window tables (tens of
minutes to hours of CPU) are shipped precomputed and loaded instead. The
specification for each is given in its own section (see
[Reproducibility and the cache]), and the dual-regime rolling calibration can be
re-run in place by knitting with

```r
rmarkdown::render("lpplsF_guide.Rmd", params = list(recompute = TRUE))
```

**Interactive surfaces.** The SSE landscapes are interactive `plotly` surfaces
(drag to rotate). `sse_surface_plot(..., static = TRUE)` draws the same grids as
static base-R `persp()` surfaces, which is how the package's PDF overview,
`vignette("lpplsF")`, shows them.

# The model and its calibration landscape

The core generator is `eval_lppls()`. A single LPPLS trajectory is a
deterministic function of a critical time $t_c$, the power-law exponent $m$, the
log-periodic angular frequency $\omega$, and linear coefficients $A, B, C_1, C_2$:

```{r intro-eval}
## ten points spread across a series whose critical time is tc = 1001
round(eval_lppls(seq(1, 1000, length.out = 10),
                 A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
                 tc = 1001, m = 0.6, omega = 8), 4)
```

Calibration means minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE) between the model
and observed log-prices over the nonlinear parameters $(t_c, m, \omega)$; the
linear parameters are profiled out. Before fitting, it helps to *see* that SSE
landscape. `sse_surface_plot()` evaluates the SSE over a grid of two parameters,
holding the rest fixed, and draws that surface. Give the values of the
parameters you are not scanning, name the two you are, and give each a range:

```{r surface-usage, eval=FALSE}
sse_surface_plot(
  log_p, t_obs,
  params = list(tc = 1001, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001),
  vary   = c("m", "omega"),
  span   = list(m = c(0.1, 0.9), omega = c(6, 13)),
  mode   = 0
)
```

Every surface in this section is produced that way. `sse_contour_plot()`, which
it wraps, returns the grid itself and can draw a contour plot of it as well.

## Simulated LPPLS(0) data

*Thesis Figure 10.* A single LPPLS(0) process (the Filimonov–Sornette
parameterization, `mode = 0`) of length $N = 1000$ plus Gaussian noise
($\sigma = 0.05$); the SSE is evaluated on the first 910 observations (the
critical time $t_c = 1001$ lies beyond the fitting window).

| $t_c$ | $m$ | $\omega$ | $A$ | $B$ | $C_1$ | $C_2$ |
|----:|----:|------:|---:|------:|------:|-----:|
| 1001 | 0.6 | 8 | 8 | -0.025 | 0.0015 | 0.001 |

```{r fig61-simulate}
set.seed(3630)
sigma <- 0.05
N     <- 1000
tc    <- N + 1                      # 1001
sim   <- vapply(1:N, function(i) {
  eval_lppls(i, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
             tc = tc, m = 0.6, omega = 8) + rnorm(1) * sigma
}, numeric(1))

log_p <- sim[1:910]                 # fitting window
t_obs <- (1:N)[1:910]
```

### SSE over $m$ and $\omega$ — thesis Figure 10(a)

Flat/low for small $m$, a weak depression near $m = 0.6$, then a steep rise for
larger $m$; only small oscillating variation along $\omega$.

```{r fig61-mo, echo=FALSE}
sse_surface_plot(
  log_p, t_obs,
  params = list(tc = 1001, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001),
  vary   = c("m", "omega"),
  span   = list(m = c(0.1, 0.9), omega = c(6, 13)), mode = 0
)
```

### SSE over $t_c$ and $m$ — thesis Figure 10(b)

Flat for small $m$, rising strongly for larger $m$; the variation along $t_c$ is
small for small $m$.

```{r fig61-tc-m, echo=FALSE}
sse_surface_plot(
  log_p, t_obs,
  params = list(omega = 8, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001),
  vary   = c("tc", "m"),
  span   = list(tc = c(N - 90 + 1, N + 90), m = c(0.1, 0.9)), mode = 0
)
```

### SSE over $t_c$ and $\omega$ — thesis Figure 10(c)

Many strong oscillations along the $\omega$ direction — the source of the
multi-modal, hard-to-optimize likelihood that motivates the profile methods below.

```{r fig61-tc-o, echo=FALSE}
sse_surface_plot(
  log_p, t_obs,
  params = list(m = 0.6, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001),
  vary   = c("tc", "omega"),
  span   = list(tc = c(N - 90 + 1, N + 90), omega = c(1, 20)), mode = 0
)
```

## Higher-order Landau variants

*Thesis Figure 11.* The package also implements the 1st- and 2nd-order
Landau expansions (`mode = 1`, `mode = 2`). In those modes $C_2$ plays the role
of the phase $\phi$, so a "$\phi$ axis" is produced by scanning $C_2$. The axes
below are labelled $\phi$ accordingly.

### $t_c$ and $\phi$, 1st-order Landau — thesis Figure 11(a)

This surface uses the **$N = 1000$ mode-0 data from the previous section**, examined under
the mode-1 $(t_c, \phi)$ landscape — modes 0 and 1 are equivalent
parameterizations of the same 1st-order Landau LPPL. The phase periodicity
($2\pi$) produces three local minima across $\phi \in [1, 20]$, plus a boundary
solution at small $\phi$.

```{r fig62-lppls1-tc-phi, echo=FALSE}
sse_surface_plot(
  log_p, t_obs,
  params = list(m = 0.6, omega = 8, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015),
  vary   = c("tc", "C2"),
  span   = list(tc = c(N - 90 + 1, N + 90), C2 = c(1, 20)), mode = 1
)
```

### A 2nd-order Landau simulation

The 2nd-order model adds a pre-critical regime of length $\Delta t = 500$ with
secondary frequency $\Delta\omega = 0$. SSE is evaluated on the first 1910 of
$N = 2000$ observations.

| $t_c$ | $m$ | $\omega$ | $A$ | $B$ | $C_1$ | $C_2$ | $\Delta t$ |
|----:|----:|------:|---:|------:|------:|-----:|----:|
| 2001 | 0.6 | 8 | 8 | -0.025 | 0.0015 | 0.001 | 500 |

```{r fig62-simulate}
set.seed(3630)
N2  <- 2000
tc2 <- N2 + 1
sim2 <- vapply(1:N2, function(i) {
  eval_lppls(i, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
             tc = tc2, m = 0.6, omega = 8, mode = 2, T1 = 500) + rnorm(1) * sigma
}, numeric(1))
log_p2 <- sim2[1:1910]
t_obs2 <- (1:N2)[1:1910]
```

### $t_c$ and $\phi$, 2nd-order Landau — thesis Figure 11(b)

Note the wider $t_c$ axis: the pre-critical regime lets parameters wander outside
the usual LPPLS filter values.

```{r fig62-lppls2-tc-phi, echo=FALSE}
sse_surface_plot(
  log_p2, t_obs2,
  params = list(m = 0.6, omega = 8, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015),
  vary   = c("tc", "C2"),
  span   = list(tc = c(N2 - 90 + 1, N2 + 200), C2 = c(1, 20)), mode = 2
)
```

### $t_c$ and $\omega$, 2nd-order Landau — thesis Figure 11(c)

Even more rugged than the Filimonov variant: narrow, deep ravines and strong
oscillations along $\omega$.

```{r fig62-lppls2-tc-o, echo=FALSE}
sse_surface_plot(
  log_p2, t_obs2,
  params = list(m = 0.6, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001),
  vary   = c("tc", "omega"),
  span   = list(tc = c(N2 - 90 + 1, N2 + 200), omega = c(1, 20)), mode = 2
)
```

# Fitting a single model

`fit_lppls()` is the workhorse. With `mode = "MPL"` it calibrates by **modified
profile likelihood**: for each candidate $t_c$ in the search window it profiles
out $(m, \omega)$ (and the linear parameters), then builds a likelihood interval
for $t_c$. We calibrate two simulated series: one with
Gaussian noise (`M1`), one with AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise (`M2`). Each holds out the
last 200 points, fits on $[1, 1800]$, and searches
$t_c$ over $[1801, 2100]$; the true $t_c = 2001$.

```{r figfit-helper}
## One-row tidy estimate table from a fit_lppls() result.
est_row <- function(fit) {
  e <- fit$fit[[1]]
  data.frame(tc = e$tc, m = e$m, omega = e$omega,
             A = unname(e$A), B = unname(e$B),
             C1 = unname(e$C1), C2 = unname(e$C2), D = unname(e$D))
}

## The calibration shared by M1 and M2. fp/pp/tp ask fit_lppls() to also attach
## the fit plot, the per-tc parameter plot and the BFGS trace plot to the
## returned object, so they are available later without refitting.
fit_call <- function(log_price) {
  fit_lppls(
    log_price = log_price, fh = 300, hold_out = 200,
    lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.03, 0.8), upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
    tc_init = 1950, m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12, num_searches = 1,
    mode = "MPL", mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5), beta_method = "crossprod",
    fp = TRUE, pp = TRUE, tp = TRUE
  )
}
```

The Gaussian series is regenerated from `set.seed(3630)`. The GARCH series ships
with this guide as `garch_series.rds`: it was drawn with `rugarch`, whose
simulated paths depend on the package version, so it is stored rather than
re-simulated.

```{r figfit-data}
set.seed(3630)
Nf <- 2000
gauss_series <- vapply(1:Nf, function(i) {
  eval_lppls(i, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
             tc = Nf + 1, m = 0.6, omega = 8) + rnorm(1) * sigma
}, numeric(1))
garch_series <- readRDS(dpath("garch_series.rds"))$log_p
```

```{r figfit-compute}
## 300 profile-likelihood optimizations per series
fit_gauss <- fit_call(gauss_series)
fit_garch <- fit_call(garch_series)
```

## The fit plot

In each plot the blue line is the simulated series, the red curve the estimated
LPPLS process (up to the estimated $t_c$), the green dashed line marks
$T_2 = 1800$, and the red dashed line the estimated $t_c$. *Thesis Figure 13;
the estimates are those of thesis Table 3.*

### M1 — Gaussian noise — thesis Figure 13(a)

```{r figfit-gauss, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Simulated log-price series with Gaussian noise over 2,000 time steps in
#|   blue, closely tracked by the fitted LPPLS curve in red. Dashed lines mark T2
#|   = 1800 in green and the estimated critical time in red, near the end of the
#|   series.
fit_gauss$fit_plot
```

```{r figfit-gauss-est}
knitr::kable(est_row(fit_gauss), digits = 5,
             caption = "M1 (Gaussian noise) estimate; tc_hat = 1996.")
```

### M2 — AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise — thesis Figure 13(b)

```{r figfit-garch, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The simulated series with AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise in blue and its fitted
#|   LPPLS curve in red, with dashed lines at T2 = 1800 in green and at the
#|   estimated critical time in red, a little earlier than in the Gaussian case.
fit_garch$fit_plot
```

```{r figfit-garch-est}
knitr::kable(est_row(fit_garch), digits = 5,
             caption = "M2 (AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise) estimate; tc_hat = 1980.")
```

## Reading the fit: `print()` diagnostics

A calibration can look perfectly good as a plot and still be untrustworthy. The
`print()` method for `fit_lppls()` reports the estimate together with the checks
that decide whether it means anything — this is the fastest way to find out
whether a fit is worth interpreting.

```{r figfit-print}
fit_gauss
```

Line by line:

* **Bounds.** $(m, \omega)$ are optimised inside a box. If the optimum sits *on*
  a wall, the SSE is still falling in that direction and the estimate is a
  constrained one — the regularity conditions behind the modified profile
  likelihood do not hold, and its intervals mean nothing. The check is reported
  twice: for the point estimate, and as a count across all the per-$t_c$
  conditional fits. The second matters on its own, because an interior point
  estimate can still rest on a profile that is pinned nearly everywhere.
* **Basins.** Each candidate $t_c$ gets its own $(m, \omega)$ search, and with
  few restarts some land in a worse local optimum than others. Distance from the
  best SSE will not detect this — the conditional SSE *should* rise away from the
  optimal $t_c$, so a healthy profile also has fits well above the minimum. What
  betrays a failed search is a **gap**: the sorted SSEs falling into a good
  cluster and a distinctly worse one. The reported number is the largest gap
  between consecutive sorted values as a share of the total spread, which is
  scale-free and near zero for a smooth profile.
* **Filters.** How many candidate fits were rejected for $B \ge 0$ or for
  damping, $D$, below its floor. These are the two constraints `fit_lppls()`
  reports internally, otherwise visible only as warnings while the fit runs.
* **MPL.** How much of the $t_c$ grid the modified profile likelihood is defined
  on. It is `NA` wherever $\det(X'X - H) \le 0$, which at a constrained optimum
  carries no guarantee of sign.

A `Diagnostics:` block of `!` lines appears only when something is wrong, so a
clean fit prints none — as here. [The S&P 500 example](#what-print-says-about-this-one) shows one that prints six.

```{r figfit-print-garch}
fit_garch
```

## Per-$t_c$ parameter estimates — thesis Figure 14

Passing `pp = TRUE` to `fit_lppls()` attaches a parameter plot: each estimated
parameter (and the objective) as a function of the candidate $t_c$, with the
objective minimum ($\hat t_c$) marked. $C_1$ and $C_2$ trace near-sinusoidal
curves that distort far from the true $t_c$ — more so under GARCH noise. No extra
calibration runs; these reuse the fits above.

### M1 — Gaussian noise — thesis Figure 14(a)

```{r param-gauss, fig.width=5, fig.height=8}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Eight stacked panels, one each for A, B, C1, C2, D, m, omega and the
#|   objective value, plotted against the candidate critical time from 1800 to
#|   2100, with a red vertical line at the estimate. A, B, D, m and omega change
#|   smoothly, C1 and C2 oscillate, and the objective is lowest at the red line.
fit_gauss$param_plot
```

### M2 — AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise — thesis Figure 14(b)

```{r param-garch, fig.width=5, fig.height=8}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The same eight panels for the AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) series: each estimate against
#|   the candidate critical time, with a red vertical line at the estimate. C1
#|   and C2 again oscillate, more distorted than under Gaussian noise.
fit_garch$param_plot
```

# Reading the optimizer: BFGS traces

*Thesis Figure 15.* With `tp = TRUE`, `fit_lppls()` attaches a trace plot. It
shows the SSE landscape over $(m, \omega)$ at the estimated $t_c$, overlaid with
the BFGS path — red dot at the start
$(m_{\text{init}}, \omega_{\text{init}}) = (0.2, 12)$, green diamond at the
estimate.

$B$ and the damping $D$ are not search coordinates. At every point of the
landscape they follow from the least-squares solution for the linear parameters,
so the plot shows them as regions instead: shaded where that solution would be
out of range, black for $B \ge 0$ and white for $D$ below its floor of 0.8, each
edged with a dashed line. The conditions are checked only where a search ends,
so a path may cross a shaded region on its way.

## $(m, \omega)$ topology — thesis Figure 15

The governing topology for calibration: a single interior minimum BFGS finds
easily. The GARCH minimum sits slightly further from the true $(0.6, 8)$. In
both, the white lobe at small $m$ is where the damping would fall below 0.8, and
the Gaussian path touches its edge on the way to the estimate. $B$ is negative
across the whole box, so nothing is shaded black.

```{r trace-mo-gauss, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Heat map of the SSE over m from 0.1 to 0.9 and omega from 6 to 13, with
#|   white contour lines around a single interior basin. An orange optimiser path
#|   runs from the red start point at m = 0.2, omega = 12 to a green diamond at
#|   the estimate near m = 0.6, omega = 8. A white shaded lobe at small m,
#|   between omega 7.5 and 10, marks where the damping would fall below 0.8; the
#|   path touches its edge.
fit_gauss$trace_plot   # Gauss
```

```{r trace-mo-garch, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The same SSE heat map over m and omega for the AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) series: a
#|   single basin, with the optimiser path from the red start point to a green
#|   diamond at the estimate, slightly further from the true m = 0.6, omega = 8.
#|   A similar white lobe at small m marks where the damping would fall below 0.8.
fit_garch$trace_plot   # GARCH
```

# Robustness to noise

*Thesis Figures 18, 19 and 20.* How much noise can a calibration take before its
estimates stop meaning anything? That is a property of the model rather than of
any particular series, so it is studied on a known signal: take a deterministic
LPPLS path, add noise at a range of levels, recalibrate at each, and watch the
estimates move.

`lppls_noise_sweep()` runs that experiment. It takes the clean signal, a vector
of noise levels, and the arguments to pass to `fit_lppls()`, and returns one row
per level:

```{r noise-sweep-usage, eval=FALSE}
N      <- 2000
signal <- eval_lppls(seq_len(N), A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
                     tc = N + 1, m = 0.6, omega = 8)

sweep <- lppls_noise_sweep(
  signal,
  sd_seq   = seq(0.005, 0.100, by = 0.005),      # 20 noise levels
  fit_args = list(fh = 150, hold_out = 100,
                  lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.03, 0.8),
                  upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
                  m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12, num_searches = 1,
                  mode = "MPL", mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5)),
  seed = 3630
)
```

The `noise` argument decides what kind of perturbation is studied. It defaults to
`rnorm`, and takes any function of `n` returning standardised innovations, so a
heavy-tailed or serially dependent alternative can be compared against the
Gaussian case on the very same signal:

```{r noise-sweep-alt, eval=FALSE}
## Student-t innovations, rescaled to unit variance so `sd_seq` still reads as
## a standard deviation
heavy <- function(n) rt(n, df = 4) / sqrt(4 / 2)
lppls_noise_sweep(signal, sd_seq = seq(0.005, 0.100, by = 0.005),
                  noise = heavy, fit_args = fit_args, seed = 3630)
```

The four sweeps below are of that shape: M1 and M2 under Gaussian noise, and the
same pair under AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise, where M2 is M1 with $C_1, C_2$ negated
(opposite phase). That is **80 calibrations**, so the tables are shipped
precomputed (`noise_*.rds`) and loaded here; see
[Reproducibility and the cache].

```{r noise-setup, echo=FALSE}
noise_m1_gauss <- readRDS(dpath("noise_m1_gauss.rds"))
noise_m2_gauss <- readRDS(dpath("noise_m2_gauss.rds"))
noise_m1_garch <- readRDS(dpath("noise_m1_garch.rds"))
noise_m2_garch <- readRDS(dpath("noise_m2_garch.rds"))
```

## Parameter estimates vs noise level — thesis Figure 18

`noise_param_plot()` draws each estimate against the noise level, one panel per
parameter. $\omega, C_1, C_2$ (the log-periodic parameters) are the most
noise-sensitive.

### Gaussian noise, M1

```{r noise-sd-gauss, fig.width=5, fig.height=8}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Six stacked panels showing the estimates of m, omega, A, B, C1 and C2
#|   against the noise standard deviation, from 0.005 to 0.1, for M1 under
#|   Gaussian noise. Each drifts steadily as the noise grows; C1 roughly halves
#|   and C2 changes sign, while m barely moves.
noise_param_plot(noise_m1_gauss)
```

### AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise, M1

```{r noise-sd-garch, fig.width=5, fig.height=8}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The same six panels for M1 under AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise: each estimate
#|   against the noise standard deviation, with the log-periodic parameters
#|   omega, C1 and C2 again the most sensitive.
noise_param_plot(noise_m1_garch)
```

## $t_c$ likelihood intervals vs noise level

`noise_tc_plot()` draws the $t_c$ estimate and the MPLE with the nested
likelihood-interval bands. Pass `true_tc` on a simulated signal and it marks the
true value, here $t_c = 2001$.

### Gaussian noise: M1, then M2 at opposite phase — thesis Figure 19

```{r noise-li-m1-gauss, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The estimated critical time against the noise standard deviation for M1
#|   under Gaussian noise. The PLE and MPLE lines coincide and fall from about
#|   2000 to about 1978 as the noise grows, inside nested likelihood-interval
#|   bands that widen with it. A dashed line marks the true value, 2001, which
#|   stays inside the widest band.
noise_tc_plot(noise_m1_gauss, true_tc = 2001)
```

```{r noise-li-m2-gauss, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The same plot for M2, at opposite phase. Under Gaussian noise the PLE and
#|   MPLE rise from about 2002 to about 2018 as the noise grows, inside
#|   likelihood-interval bands that widen with it, while the true value, 2001,
#|   stays just below the lower edge of the innermost band.
noise_tc_plot(noise_m2_gauss, true_tc = 2001)
```

### AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise: M1, then M2 at opposite phase — thesis Figure 20

```{r noise-li-m1-garch, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The estimated critical time and its likelihood-interval bands against the
#|   noise standard deviation for M1 under AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise, with a dashed
#|   line at the true value, 2001.
noise_tc_plot(noise_m1_garch, true_tc = 2001)
```

```{r noise-li-m2-garch, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The estimated critical time and its likelihood-interval bands against the
#|   noise standard deviation for M2 under AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) noise, with a dashed
#|   line at the true value, 2001.
noise_tc_plot(noise_m2_garch, true_tc = 2001)
```

# Rolling windows and Lagrange regularization

*Thesis Figures 23 to 25.* Lagrange regularization (Demos & Sornette, 2019)
tries to find the onset of a bubble by rolling the calibration start $T_1$
forward (fixed end $T_2$) and looking for the window where the normalized
residual $\chi^2_{np}(T_1)$ stops falling. The package
splits this into a reusable primitive and cheap post-processing:

* `lppls_rolling()` runs one calibration per $T_1$ (the expensive part);
* `lppls_lagrange()`, `rolling_tc_plot()`, `rolling_param_plot()`,
  `chi_sq_np_plot()`, `chi_sq_lambda_plot()` are all post-processing on it.

In a pure LPPL process every window is already LPPL, so $\chi^2_{np}$ is flat and
regularization has nothing to correct. So the example is a **dual-regime** series
consisting of a flat "ranging" segment for $t < 600$ that switches to an LPPL
process at $t = 600$
(`tc = 2001, m = 0.6, omega = 8, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001`;
Gaussian noise $\sigma = 0.05$, seed 3630). The rolling approaches the onset from
below: as $T_1$ climbs toward 600 each window sheds more of the pre-LPPL data and
the fit tightens, so $\chi^2_{np}$ decreases; once $T_1$ passes 600 the window is
pure LPPL again and the trend flattens. The rolling ($T_1 = 1 \to 1001$ step 10,
$T_2 = 1900$; 101 windows) is shipped precomputed as
`lagrange_rolling_regime_gauss.rds`.

```{r regime-gauss-build}
## The dual-regime series: flat at the LPPL value at t = 600 for t < 600, then
## the LPPL process itself, with N(0, 0.05^2) noise throughout. In this example
## the two segments draw their noise from separate seeds: `seed` for the flat
## prefix, `seed + 1` for the bubble. So both set.seed() calls are needed to
## reproduce it. (This is not really important, it just happens to be the way
## the figures for the thesis were generated.)
N_rg <- 2000
build_rg <- function(seed, onset = 600) {
  bub <- eval_lppls(onset:N_rg, 8, -0.025, 0.0015, 0.001, N_rg + 1, 0.6, 8)
  set.seed(seed + 1)
  c(rep(bub[1], onset - 1), bub) +
    c({ set.seed(seed); rnorm(onset - 1) * 0.05 }, rnorm(N_rg - onset + 1) * 0.05)
}

## Regenerated on both paths: it is instant, and the residual guard below needs
## the series even when the calibration comes from the cache.
lp_rg <- build_rg(3630)
```

```{r regime-gauss-compute, eval=RECOMPUTE}
## 101 windows, each a 150-candidate tc scan (MPL: the likelihood
## intervals rolling_tc_plot() needs).
roll_rg <- lppls_rolling(
  lp_rg,
  t1_seq = seq(1, 1001, by = 10),
  hold_out = 100,
  fh = 150,
  fit_args = list(
    lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.03, 0.8),
    upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
    m_init = 0.2,
    o_init = 12,
    num_searches = 1,
    mode = "MPL",
    mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5),
    factr = 1e7)
  )
```

```{r regime-gauss-save, eval=RECOMPUTE, echo=FALSE}
saveRDS(roll_rg, dpath("lagrange_rolling_regime_gauss.rds"))
```

```{r regime-gauss-load, eval=!RECOMPUTE, echo=FALSE}
roll_rg <- readRDS(dpath("lagrange_rolling_regime_gauss.rds"))
```

```{r regime-gauss-lagrange}
lag_rg <- lppls_lagrange(roll_rg, p = 0)
lag_rg
```

Optimal $T_1^* =$ **`r lag_rg$t1_star`** (true onset 600); $\lambda =$
`r signif(-lag_rg$slope, 3)` $> 0$ — a genuine bias trend (a pure LPPL series
would give $\lambda \approx 0$).

`lppls_rolling()` keeps the fit from every window. To examine the one that
Lagrange regularization selected, locate it in the sequence and pull out the
quantities that describe it.

```{r regime-gauss-window}
k_rg  <- which(roll_rg$t1_seq == lag_rg$t1_star)  # position of the optimal window
T1_rg <- roll_rg$t1_seq[k_rg]                     # its calibration start, T1*
nc_rg <- roll_rg$table$n_cal[k_rg]                # how many points it calibrated on
T2_rg <- T1_rg + nc_rg - 1                        # its calibration end, T2
f_rg  <- roll_rg$fits[[k_rg]]                     # the fit itself
```

## The generated series and its fit — thesis Figure 23

Blue the generated series, red the fitted LPPLS process up to $\hat t_c$, dashed
markers at the calibration bounds and $\hat t_c$. The series spans two regimes and
the fit is calibrated on only the later part, so the red curve starts at $T_1^*$ —
the flat regime is shown but never fitted. `lppls_rolling()` stores the fit in
window-local time ($t = 1$ at $T_1$), so $\hat t_c$ is shifted by the window offset
to draw it on the global clock.

```{r regime-gauss-fit, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The dual-regime series in blue, flat with noise up to t = 600 and then
#|   rising as an LPPLS bubble to t = 2000. The fitted LPPLS curve in red starts
#|   at the selected T1, marked by an orange dashed line, and ends at the
#|   estimated critical time, marked in red; a green dashed line marks T2 = 1900.
f_glob    <- f_rg
f_glob$tc <- f_rg$tc + (T1_rg - 1)   # window-local -> global clock

fit_plot(f_glob, seq_along(lp_rg), lp_rg, T1 = T1_rg, T2 = T2_rg)
```

Give `fit_plot()` both window bounds and it draws the curve only where the fit
applies.

## Rolling-$T_1$ estimates — thesis Figure 24

How the $t_c$ estimate and the six parameters move as $T_1$ rolls across the
onset. For $T_1$ well below 600 the window still contains ranging data and the
estimates wander; as $T_1$ approaches and passes 600 the window becomes
predominantly, then purely, LPPL and $\hat t_c$ settles near the true 2001.

```{r regime-gauss-tc, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The estimated critical time against the window start T1, from 1 to 1001,
#|   with nested likelihood-interval bands. It jumps between about 1930 and 2050
#|   while the windows still hold much of the flat regime, then climbs and
#|   settles near 1990 once T1 passes about 600, where the widest bands contain
#|   the true value, 2001.
rolling_tc_plot(roll_rg)
```

```{r regime-gauss-params, fig.width=5, fig.height=8}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Six stacked panels showing A, B, C1, C2, m and omega against the window
#|   start T1. All six jump erratically for T1 below about 270, then settle: A
#|   near 8, B just below 0, C1 and C2 close to 0, m rising to about 0.6, and
#|   omega rising to about 8 by T1 = 600.
rolling_param_plot(roll_rg)
```

## Lagrange regularization — thesis Figure 25

$\chi^2_{np}(T_1)$ with the OLS bias trend (red), then the regularized objective
$\chi^2_{\lambda^*}(T_1)$ with the optimal $T_1^*$ (green):

```{r regime-gauss-chi-np, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Scatter of the normalised residual chi-squared against T1 with a red fitted
#|   linear trend sloping downward. The points fall from about 0.006 at T1 = 0 to
#|   about 0.0024 by T1 = 570, scattered in two tiers below T1 = 270, and stay
#|   flat after that.
chi_sq_np_plot(lag_rg)
```

```{r regime-gauss-chi-lambda, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Scatter of the regularised objective against T1, V-shaped with its minimum
#|   near T1 = 500, where a green vertical line marks the optimal T1*. Below T1 =
#|   270 the points scatter in two tiers.
chi_sq_lambda_plot(lag_rg)
```

> **Is that decrease real, or a noise artifact?** That question, and the
> autocorrelation-robust `lr_trend_test()` that answers it, are taken up in a
> separate investigation,
> [`lagrange_inference_report.Rmd`](https://github.com/mahovo/lpplsF/blob/main/misc/lagrange_inference_report.Rmd),
> in the package's `misc/` directory on GitHub. It is not built with the package.

## Residuals at $T_1^*$

```{r regime-gauss-guard, echo=FALSE}
## Load-path integrity: the regenerated series must reproduce the cached
## calibration exactly (residual SSE == stored sse_cal).
res_rg <- lp_rg[T1_rg:roll_rg$n_full][seq_len(nc_rg)] -
  eval_lppls(seq_len(nc_rg), f_rg$A, f_rg$B, f_rg$C1, f_rg$C2,
             f_rg$tc, f_rg$m, f_rg$omega, mode = 0)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(res_rg^2), roll_rg$table$sse_cal[k_rg])))
```

The residual QQ plot for the window at $T_1^*$. The residuals are near-normal.

```{r regime-gauss-res, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Normal QQ plot of the residuals of the window at T1*, with a red reference
#|   line and green lines at the 10% and 90% quantiles. The points lie on the
#|   line except for slight departures in the extreme tails.
residual_qq_plot(res_rg)
```

# Empirical example: the S&P 500

*Thesis Figures 27 to 32.* The package ships the S&P 500 series as the dataset `spx` (see
`?spx`), covering exactly the calibrated window, 2009-05-18 to 2020-12-31. We fit
on $[1, 2428]$ (to 2019-01-08) with `hold_out = 500`, `fh = 500`.

```{r spx-data}
## `spx` is lazy-loaded with the package: 2,928 daily closes, 2009-05-18..2020-12-31.
df_spx <- data.frame(Date = spx$date, logpris = log(spx$close))
df_spx$ID <- seq_len(nrow(df_spx))
n_cal_spx <- nrow(df_spx) - 500    # 2428
```

> **A note on the series.** The thesis calibrated the CRSP S&P 500 Composite
> series (`spindx`, obtained through Wharton Research Data Services). That data
> is licensed and cannot be redistributed, so the package ships the corresponding
> Yahoo Finance series (`^GSPC`) for the same trading days. The two agree to
> 1.6e-07 on average, and recalibrating on the shipped series leaves every
> quantity reported below unchanged: $\hat t_c = 2717$ (2020-03-03), $m = 0.9$,
> $\omega = 6.1596$, and all three likelihood intervals identical. Only the
> Brent-refined $t_c$ at the final step of the MPL computation moves, in its
> seventh decimal. That step refines thesis equation 38 at the
> $(\hat m, \hat\omega)$ which minimise equation 39 on the integer grid.

```{r spx-compute}
## fh = 500 profile-likelihood optimizations
spx_fit <- fit_lppls(
  log_price = df_spx$logpris, fh = 500, hold_out = 500,
  lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.5, 0.8), upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
  tc_init = n_cal_spx + 250, m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12, num_searches = 1,
  mode = "MPL", mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5),
  dates = df_spx$Date,          # calendar labels for the 1..n index
  style = "empirical",          # grey data; the forecast past T2 in red
  fp = TRUE, mpl_plot = TRUE, tp = TRUE, pp = TRUE)
```

```{r spx-est}
e <- spx_fit$fit[[1]]
```

The point estimate: PLE $t_c =$
**`r as.character(df_spx$Date[round(e$tc)])`**, with $m =$ `r round(e$m, 2)`
(pinned at the upper boundary) and $\omega =$ `r round(e$omega, 2)`.

### What `print()` says about this one

[Reading the fit](#reading-the-fit-print-diagnostics) introduced the diagnostics on a healthy calibration, which printed no
warnings. This is the contrasting case, and it is worth reading before any of the
figures below:

```{r spx-print}
spx_fit
```

Six flags, and every caveat in the rest of this section follows from them. The
estimate is a **boundary solution**, and not marginally — $m$ is at its upper
bound in the point estimate *and* in every conditional fit, with
$\partial\,\mathrm{SSE}/\partial m < 0$ there, so the constraint is genuinely
active and the regularity conditions behind the modified profile likelihood do
not hold. Most of the conditional fits sit in a **distinctly inferior basin**,
which is why the MPL curve below is two-tiered rather than smooth, and why
`num_searches = 1` is the wrong setting for this series. And the MPL is
**undefined on part of the grid**, so the curve has gaps the likelihood intervals
cannot see across.

The last three are about the likelihood intervals themselves. LI(0.05) and
LI(0.10) each **bridge grid points** that are not above their cutoff, and every
$t_c$ inside an interval is a **good-basin fit**, so the intervals trace where the
search succeeded rather than the curvature of the likelihood.
[The modified profile likelihood](#modified-profile-likelihood-thesis-figure-28)
below takes this up.

None of this is visible in the point estimate, which looks entirely ordinary.

It would be easy to read the warnings above as a defect in the data, in the
settings, or in the package, and to go looking for a configuration that silences
them. That would be the wrong lesson. Boundary solutions, split basins and an
undefined modified profile likelihood are *properties of the LPPLS model itself*:
the objective is non-convex, the log-periodic parameters are only weakly
identified, and the regularity conditions the modified profile likelihood assumes
are not guaranteed to hold at a constrained optimum.

The master's thesis for which this package was written takes up exactly this
question: When an LPPLS calibration is worth believing, and what to do when it is
not. The S&P 500 case above is its Chapter 9.

## Fit plot — thesis Figure 27

Because the calibration was given `dates`, the attached `$fit_plot` is already
drawn on a calendar axis. Pass `dates` to [`fit_lppls()`] and every plot and
printout it produces speaks in dates; omit it and everything falls back to the
1..n time index.

It was also given `style = "empirical"`. An observed price series is given and
cannot be otherwise, so it is drawn in grey, and the fitted curve splits at
$T_2$: blue where data supports it, red beyond, where the curve is a forecast.
The default `style = "simulated"` draws a generated series in colour with a
single fitted line, which is what the earlier sections use.

```{r spx-fitplot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The S&P 500 log price from 2009 to 2020 in grey, with the fitted LPPLS curve
#|   in blue up to T2 in January 2019 and its forecast continuation in red up to
#|   the estimated critical time in March 2020. Dashed vertical lines mark T2 in
#|   blue and the critical time in red; the index crashes around the critical
#|   time and then recovers.
plot(spx_fit, "fit")
```

The same plot can be drawn from a bare estimate with `fit_plot()`, which takes
`dates` directly:

```{r spx-fitplot-direct, eval=FALSE}
fit_plot(spx_fit$fit[[1]], seq_len(nrow(df_spx)), df_spx$logpris,
         T2 = n_cal_spx, dates = df_spx$Date, style = "empirical")
```

## Modified profile likelihood — thesis Figure 28

The MPLE coincides with the PLE, at 2020-03-03. The `MPL:` line of the printout
above gives that date next to the index, and each likelihood interval in both
forms. The modified profile likelihood is `NA` wherever $\det(X'X - H) \le 0$. At a
constrained optimum that determinant carries no guarantee of sign, which is why
the same line counted gaps in the grid.

> **Diagnostic caveat.** The point estimate agrees with the PLE, but the bands are
> not inference — the `Bounds:` and `Basins:` lines above already say why. Two
> consequences the printed summary does not spell out. First, the basin split is
> what makes the curve **two-tiered** rather than smooth: the two tiers are
> $\approx 500$ log-likelihood units apart, so the plot below is not one curve but
> two.
>
> Second, and the reason to distrust the bands specifically: the likelihood
> intervals here trace **where the optimiser succeeded**, not the curvature of the
> likelihood. Every grid point inside LI_05 is a good-basin fit and every point
> outside it is not; its lower edge is exactly where the good-basin run containing
> the PLE begins, and its upper edge is the end of the *next* such run, which
> `range()` bridges across the gap between them. LI_05 and LI_10 coincide for the
> same reason. The relative-scale plot below makes this visible: only LI_50 has a
> crossing. **Read the MPLE, not the bands.**

```{r spx-mplplot, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The log modified profile likelihood of the S&P 500 fit against candidate
#|   critical times from about 2460 to 2930, in two tiers roughly 500 units
#|   apart, with gaps: an upper tier peaking in a short plateau near 7383 around
#|   the estimate, and a long lower tier between about 6770 and 6890. Vertical
#|   lines mark the PLE, the MPLE and the bounds of the 5%, 10% and 50%
#|   likelihood intervals.
spx_fit$mpl_plot
```

### The same curve on a relative scale

The absolute level of the log MPL carries no information. Its magnitude comes
almost entirely from the variance term of the modified profile likelihood
(thesis eq. 53), $-\tfrac{n - p - 2}{2}\log \hat{s}_{t_c}$. A well-fitting model has a small
residual variance, here $\hat{s} = \sigma^2 \approx 0.0022$, whose logarithm is
large and negative. Multiplying by $-(n - p - 2)/2 \approx -1210$ flips the sign
and scales it by the sample size, which gives $\approx 7417$. The determinant
ratio contributes only $\approx -34$, so the curve peaks near $7383$. The formula
also drops additive constants that do not depend on $t_c$. What the likelihood intervals actually test is the *difference*
$R = \log\mathrm{MPL} - \max\log\mathrm{MPL}$ against $\log(\text{cutoff})$, and
the fit already stores it as `mpl_output$R`.

Plotting $R$ and restricting the view to the band the cutoffs live in provides a
better view of the optimum. `plot(fit, "mpl_relative")` draws that view from the
stored `mpl_output`, so it needs nothing requested at fit time. The horizontal
lines are the cutoffs themselves, so each interval can be read off where the
curve crosses one.

```{r spx-mplplot-rel, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The same curve on a relative scale, log MPL minus its maximum, with
#|   horizontal lines at the cutoffs log 0.5, log 0.1 and log 0.05. The curve
#|   exists only between about 2696 and 2757: it peaks at 0 at the estimate and
#|   falls to about -1.15, so it crosses only the log 0.5 line.
plot(spx_fit, "mpl_relative")
```

Only `LI_50` has a crossing: the curve descends from the peak to about $-1.15$
and then stops, so it never reaches $\log 0.10$ or $\log 0.05$. Those two
intervals end where the good basin ends.

## The rest of the diagnostics

`print()` is the quick triage. Three further tools answer the questions it
raises: *where* the basins are, whether the estimate sits at a genuine minimum,
and whether the intervals are closed by the likelihood or by the grid.

### The basin split, drawn

`plot(fit, "basin")` shows every conditional fit's SSE against its $t_c$, split
at the gap `print()` reported. It needs nothing that was not already computed, so
it works even on a fit that requested no plots.

```{r spx-basin, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.6}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   SSE of each conditional fit against its candidate critical time, coloured by
#|   basin: short runs of good-basin fits in blue with SSE between about 5.3 and
#|   6, and inferior-basin fits in red with SSE between about 8 and 9 covering
#|   most of the grid.
plot(spx_fit, "basin")
```

The same view of the well-behaved calibration from [Fitting a single model](#fitting-a-single-model), for contrast — one cloud,
rising smoothly away from the optimal $t_c$, which is what a profile should look
like:

```{r gauss-basin, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.6}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The same view for the Gaussian-noise calibration: a single smooth curve of
#|   conditional fits with no distinct inferior cluster, falling from about 4.9
#|   at tc = 1800 to a minimum near 2000 and rising again toward 2100.
plot(fit_gauss, "basin")
```

### What the basins are made of

The view above shows *that* the fits split, but not what they split on.
`"param_basin"` applies the same division to every estimated parameter rather
than only the objective, which is where the mechanism becomes visible.

```{r spx-param-basin, fig.width=6, fig.height=9.5}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Eight stacked panels showing A, B, C1, C2, D, m, omega and the objective
#|   value of every conditional fit against its candidate critical time, coloured
#|   by basin, with a red vertical line at the estimate. The basins separate most
#|   clearly in omega, near 6 for the good fits and between 10 and 13 for the
#|   inferior ones, while m is 0.9 in both; the inferior fits' C1 and C2
#|   oscillate rapidly and the good ones trace smooth arcs.
plot(spx_fit, "param_basin")
```

```{r spx-basin-ranges}
## The split is the one summary() reports; here it is per parameter.
cut_at <- summary(spx_fit)$split_at[1]
pt     <- spx_fit$fit[[2]]
pt$basin <- ifelse(pt$value <= cut_at, "good", "inferior")
rng <- function(z) sprintf("%.3f - %.3f", min(z), max(z))
knitr::kable(
  aggregate(cbind(m, omega, D) ~ basin, data = pt, FUN = rng),
  caption = "Range of each nonlinear estimate within each basin.")
```

The two basins are separated almost entirely by $\omega$: The good one sits near
the bottom of the $[6, 13]$ search box, the inferior one near the top. $m$ is at
$0.9$ in **both**, so it plays no part in the split at all.

That separates two failures which the SSE view alone runs together. The pinned
$m$ is a **boundary** problem, and it affects every fit on the grid. The two
tiers are an **$\omega$ multimodality** problem, and it affects only which
optimum a single L-BFGS-B start happens to reach — a `num_searches` setting, not
a property of the data. The `C1`/`C2` facets tell the same story: The inferior
fits oscillate through a high-frequency regime while the good ones trace a smooth
low-frequency arc.

### Curvature at the estimate

The modified profile likelihood assumes the estimate is an interior minimum: Its
correction uses $\det(X'X - H)$, the observed information, which is only
guaranteed positive at an interior stationary point. $X$ holds the model's first
derivatives with respect to the six parameters, and $H$ its second derivatives,
each weighted by the residual at that observation and summed (thesis eq. 55).
$H$ is thus a residual-weighted curvature term rather than a Hessian in its own
right. `lppls_curvature()` tests the determinant directly, and factorises it to
show where the sign comes from.

By the Schur complement, $\det(X'X - H)$ factorises into the determinant of the
linear-parameter block times the determinant of the $2 \times 2$ Hessian of the
$(m, \omega)$ profile. The model is linear in $A, B, C_1, C_2$, so their second
derivatives vanish, $H$ contributes nothing to the linear block, and what remains
there is a crossproduct with a positive determinant. The sign is therefore
decided entirely by curvature in the two nonlinear parameters: the
$2 \times 2$ block the function reports.

```{r spx-curvature}
lppls_curvature(spx_fit)
```

Read the classification and the bound note as two separate facts. The curvature
*is* positive definite here, so the $t_c$ the MPL reports is not an artefact of a
degenerate Hessian. But $m$ rests on its bound, so the gradient need not vanish:
the estimate is a constrained one whatever the curvature says. It is the
combination of sound curvature and an active constraint that makes the point
estimate usable and the intervals not.

### Everything at once: `summary()`

`summary()` returns the diagnostics as values rather than text, so they can be
tested against instead of parsed. Printing it gives the `print()` report plus the
curvature line and an interval breakdown.

```{r spx-summary}
s <- summary(spx_fit)
s$basin_gap
s$mpl$li_check[[1]]
```

That last list is the interval integrity check. `fit_lppls()` forms each interval
as `range()` of the $t_c$ whose $R$ exceeds $\log(\text{cutoff})$ — and `range()`
does not care whether that set has holes. When it does, the reported interval
contains grid points that are not themselves in it:

```{r spx-summary-print}
s
```

`LI(0.05)` and `LI(0.10)` each span more grid points than are above their cutoff:
the interval bridges the gap between two runs of good-basin fits. `LI(0.50)` is
contiguous. This is the same conclusion the relative-scale plot above shows
visually, arrived at from the numbers.

## Fit diagnostics — thesis Figure 32

The BFGS path slides to the $(m, \omega)$ boundary corner; the per-$t_c$
parameter panel shows $m$ pinned at 0.9 with jumps where it hits the boundary.

```{r spx-trace, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Heat map of the SSE over m and omega for the S&P 500 fit, falling steadily
#|   toward large m and small omega. The orange optimiser path runs straight from
#|   the red start point at m = 0.2, omega = 12 to a green diamond in the corner
#|   at m = 0.9, omega near 6, on the edge of the search box. A small white lobe
#|   in the bottom-left corner, at small m and omega, marks where the damping
#|   would fall below 0.8.
spx_fit$trace_plot
```

```{r spx-param, fig.width=5, fig.height=8}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Eight stacked panels showing each estimate of the S&P 500 calibration
#|   against the candidate critical time, with a red vertical line at the
#|   estimate. m sits at its upper bound of 0.9 for every candidate, and the
#|   other parameters jump between two branches, one for each optimisation basin.
spx_fit$param_plot
```

## Residual QQ diagnostics — thesis Figure 29

Residuals of the SPX calibration ($t < \hat t_c$) against a normal and a fitted
Student-t reference, both via `residual_qq_plot()`.

```{r spx-qq-setup, echo=FALSE}
lppls_all <- eval_lppls(df_spx$ID, e$A, e$B, e$C1, e$C2, e$tc, e$m, e$omega)
res_spx   <- df_spx$logpris[!is.na(lppls_all)] - lppls_all[!is.na(lppls_all)]
```

```{r spx-qq-norm, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Normal QQ plot of the S&P 500 calibration residuals with a red reference
#|   line and green lines at the 10% and 90% quantiles. The points follow the
#|   line in the middle but bend away from it at both ends, below it in the lower
#|   tail and above it in the upper: heavier tails than the normal.
residual_qq_plot(res_spx)
```

```{r spx-qq-t, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The same residuals against a fitted Student-t reference. The points follow
#|   the line through the middle but flatten at both ends, above it in the lower
#|   tail and below it in the upper: lighter tails than the fitted t.
residual_qq_plot(res_spx, "t")
```

## Lagrange regularization on the S&P 500 — thesis Figure 31

Rolling $T_1 = 1 \to 501$ step 25 (21 windows), $T_2 = 2428$ fixed; shipped
precomputed as `lagrange_rolling_spx.rds` (21-window MPL fit). It is the
`spx_fit` call above rolled over $T_1$, so window 1 is `spx_fit` itself:

```{r spxroll-spec, eval=FALSE}
roll_spx <- lppls_rolling(
  df_spx$logpris, t1_seq = seq(1, 501, 25), hold_out = 500, fh = 500,
  fit_args = list(lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.5, 0.8), upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
                  m_init = 0.2, o_init = 12, num_searches = 1, mode = "MPL",
                  mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5)))
```

```{r spxroll-setup}
roll_spx <- readRDS(dpath("lagrange_rolling_spx.rds"))
lag_spx  <- lppls_lagrange(roll_spx, p = 0)
lag_spx
```

Optimal $T_1^* =$ **`r lag_spx$t1_star`**
(= `r as.character(df_spx$Date[lag_spx$t1_star])`). Here $\beta_1 < 0$,
$\lambda > 0$, so the Demos bias trend is genuinely present.

```{r spxroll-chi-np, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Scatter of the normalised residual chi-squared against T1 for the 21 S&P 500
#|   rolling windows, T1 from 1 to 501. It falls from about 0.0022 to about
#|   0.0011, with a plateau between T1 = 100 and 275, and a red fitted linear
#|   trend slopes downward through it.
chi_sq_np_plot(lag_spx)
```

```{r spxroll-chi-lambda, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Scatter of the regularised objective against T1 for the S&P 500 rolling
#|   windows: irregular, lowest at T1 = 76, where a green vertical line marks the
#|   optimal T1*, with a second, slightly higher dip near T1 = 350.
chi_sq_lambda_plot(lag_spx)
```

```{r spxroll-output-T1, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   The estimated critical time against T1 for the S&P 500 rolling windows, with
#|   nested likelihood-interval bands. The PLE and MPLE climb from about 2717 at
#|   T1 = 1 to the top of the candidate grid, about 2928, by T1 = 125 and stay
#|   there, while the bands close in on the same limit.
rolling_tc_plot(roll_spx)   # PLE saturates at the tc bound
```

# Reproducibility and the cache

This document separates three tiers of computation:

1. **Live (always run).** The [SSE surfaces](#the-model-and-its-calibration-landscape), all data simulation and the
   three single-model calibrations `fit_gauss`, `fit_garch` and `spx_fit` are
   recomputed on every knit; the calibration code is shown in full above.
2. **Cached, re-runnable in place.** The dual-regime rolling calibration is
   cached as `lagrange_rolling_regime_gauss.rds`. Knit with
   `params = list(recompute = TRUE)` to re-run it and refresh the cache.
3. **Precomputed multi-fit tables (reload-only).** The 20-level noise experiments
   (`noise_*.rds`) and the S&P 500 rolling calibration
   (`lagrange_rolling_spx.rds`) are shipped precomputed. The specification for
   each is given in its own section, so they can be regenerated with
   `lppls_noise_sweep()` and `lppls_rolling()`.

The only input that cannot be regenerated deterministically is the
AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) series. `rugarch`'s simulated paths depend on the package
version, so it is always loaded from `garch_series.rds`.

```{r session, echo=FALSE}
sessionInfo()
```
